puzzles.title: Two sum
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `two_sum` returns the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: The decoy `seen[i] = num` stores the map backwards. And `seen[num] = i` has to come after the check, or a number can match itself: try `[3, 3]` with target 6.

puzzles.title: Largest number
puzzles.prompt: `largest` should return the biggest number in a non-empty list. One line is wrong.
puzzles.why: Starting at `0` assumes some number beats zero. With all negatives, nothing does, so it returns `0`, which isn’t even in the list. Start from the first element instead.

puzzles.title: Two names, one list
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: `ys = xs` doesn’t copy anything; both names point at the same list. Appending through `ys` changes the list `xs` sees. Use `xs.copy()` or `xs[:]` for an independent list.

puzzles.title: Factorial
puzzles.prompt: `factorial(n)` should return `n!`, so `factorial(5)` is 120. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: `range` stops before its end value. Which `k` does the loop need to reach?
puzzles.why: `range(1, n)` stops at `n - 1`, so it would leave `n` itself out of the product. The end has to be `n + 1` to include it.

puzzles.title: Palindrome check
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `is_palindrome` uses two pointers to check whether `s` reads the same both ways. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: The pointers start at the ends and move toward each other, so the decoy that moves them outward would run off the string. The comparison has to happen before the pointers move, or you skip the outermost pair.

puzzles.title: Fibonacci
puzzles.prompt: `fib(n)` should return the nth Fibonacci number, where `fib(0)` is 0 and `fib(1)` is 1. One line is wrong.
puzzles.hint: Trace `fib(0)`. The loop never runs. What comes back?
puzzles.why: After `n` steps, `a` holds `fib(n)` and `b` is already one ahead. Returning `b` is off by one: `fib(0)` gives 1 and `fib(2)` gives 2.

puzzles.title: Floor division
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: `//` rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero. `7 / 2` is 3.5, floored to 3; `-7 / 2` is -3.5, floored to -4. C and Java truncate to -3 instead, which trips people moving between languages.

puzzles.title: Count vowels
puzzles.prompt: `vowels(s)` should count the vowels in a lowercase string. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: `ch` is one character and `"aeiou"` is five. You want a membership test.
puzzles.why: `in` on a string checks whether a character appears in it. `==` and `is` compare `ch` to the whole string `"aeiou"`, which never matches, and `not in` counts consonants.

puzzles.title: Reverse a linked list
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `reverse` flips a singly linked list in place and returns the new head. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: Save `curr.next` first, because the next line overwrites it. The decoy `curr.next = curr` points a node at itself and makes an infinite loop.

puzzles.title: Average
puzzles.prompt: `average` should return the mean of a non-empty list of numbers. One line is wrong.
puzzles.why: `//` is floor division, so the fractional part is thrown away: `average([1, 2])` returns `1` instead of `1.5`. Plain `/` keeps it.

puzzles.title: Sticky default
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: The default list is created once, when `def` runs. Every call that omits `acc` shares it, so the second call appends to the list the first call already filled.

puzzles.title: Reverse a string
puzzles.prompt: `reverse(s)` should return `s` backwards. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: A slice has three parts: start, stop, and step.
puzzles.why: A step of `-1` walks the string from the end to the start. `-1:` is just the last character, `::1` is the whole string forwards, and `1:` drops the first character.

puzzles.title: Binary search
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `search` returns the index of `target` in the sorted list `nums`, or -1. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: The decoy `mid = lo + hi // 2` is a precedence bug: `//` binds tighter than `+`, so it computes `lo + (hi // 2)`. The equality check comes first so the `else` only runs when the target is on the left.

puzzles.title: Shared default
puzzles.prompt: `add_item` should return a new list with `item` in it unless you pass your own `bag`. One line is wrong.
puzzles.hint: Call `add_item(1)` and then `add_item(2)`. What does the second call return?
puzzles.why: A default value is built once, when the function is defined, so every call without `bag` appends to the same list: the second call returns `[1, 2]`. Defaulting to `None` makes the `is None` check do its job.

puzzles.title: Slicing
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: Slices include the start and exclude the end. `1` starts at `h`, and `-1` is the last character `e`, which is left out, so you get `hil`.

puzzles.title: Sum of evens
puzzles.prompt: `sum_evens(nums)` should add up only the even numbers. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: What is `n % 2` for an even number?
puzzles.why: An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2, so `n % 2 == 0`. `!=` and `>` pick the odd numbers instead, and `n % 2` is never below 0 here.

puzzles.title: Max subarray
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `max_subarray` returns the largest sum of any contiguous slice of `nums` (Kadane’s algorithm). One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: At each step you either extend the current run or start fresh at `x`, which is `max(x, cur + x)`. The decoy never adds anything, so it just tracks the largest single number.

puzzles.title: Binary search
puzzles.prompt: `search` should return the index of `target` in the sorted list `xs`, or `-1` if it isn’t there. One line is wrong.
puzzles.why: `hi` is an inclusive index, so a range where `lo == hi` still holds one candidate. Stopping at `lo < hi` skips it: `search([5], 5)` never looks and returns `-1`.

puzzles.title: Late binding
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?

lines.text: fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]

puzzles.why: Each lambda looks up `i` when it is called, not when it is made. By then the loop has finished and `i` is 2. Bind it early with `lambda i=i: i` to get `[0, 1, 2]`.

puzzles.title: Clamp
puzzles.prompt: `clamp(x, lo, hi)` should return `x` limited to the range `lo` to `hi`. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: Work from the inside out. The inner call should cap `x` at `hi`.
puzzles.why: `min(x, hi)` caps `x` at the top of the range, then `max(lo, ...)` lifts it to the bottom. With `max` inside, everything comes out as at least `hi`.

puzzles.title: Dedupe a sorted array
puzzles.prompt: `nums` is sorted and non-empty. Order the lines so `dedupe` removes duplicates in place and returns how many unique values are left. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: `k` is where the next unique value goes, so you write first and then advance it. The decoy copies in the wrong direction and overwrites values you haven’t read yet.

puzzles.title: Palindrome
puzzles.prompt: `is_palindrome` should return `True` when `s` reads the same both ways, like `"racecar"`. One line is wrong.
puzzles.hint: On the first pass with `"racecar"`, what is `s[j]`?
puzzles.why: `len(s)` is one past the last index, so the very first `s[j]` raises `IndexError`. The right pointer has to start at `len(s) - 1`.

puzzles.title: Equal but not the same
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: `==` compares contents, and both lists hold `[1]`. `is` asks whether they are the same object, and two separate list literals are two separate objects.

puzzles.title: Swap
puzzles.prompt: `swap(a, b)` should return the two values the other way round. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: The right side is built in full before anything on the left is assigned.
puzzles.why: Python evaluates the right side into a tuple first, then unpacks it, so `a, b = b, a` swaps without a temporary variable.

puzzles.title: First unique character
puzzles.prompt: Order the lines so `first_unique` returns the index of the first character that appears only once in `s`, or -1. One line doesn’t belong.
puzzles.why: It takes two passes: count everything first, then scan in order for a count of 1. The decoy resets each count to 1, so every character would look unique.

puzzles.title: Dedupe, keep order
puzzles.prompt: `dedupe` should drop repeated items and keep the first of each, in order. One line is wrong.
puzzles.hint: `seen` starts empty. Does anything ever get added to it?
puzzles.why: The condition is inverted. `seen` starts empty, so `x in seen` is never true, nothing is ever added, and `dedupe` always returns `[]`. It should act on items it has not seen yet.

puzzles.title: Chained comparison
puzzles.prompt: What does this print?
puzzles.why: Python chains comparisons: `1 < 3 > 2` means `1 < 3 and 3 > 2`, which is `True`. It is not `(1 < 3) > 2`, which would be `True > 2`, or `False`.

puzzles.title: Count words
puzzles.prompt: `word_count(s)` should count the words in a sentence like `"the quick fox"`. Fill the blank.
puzzles.hint: You want a list with one item per word.
puzzles.why: `split()` with no argument breaks on runs of whitespace and returns a list of words. `strip` and `lower` return strings, so `len` would count characters.
